# Is it possible to charge a 12V car battery externally with another car battery?

The short answer is yes. Removing the dead battery from your 1991 Mazda MX-5 and charging it externally with jumper cables connected to a donor vehicle is a safe and standard procedure, provided you follow the correct polarity and connection order. The fact that the battery was previously connected to the starter motor, alternator, and ECU does not introduce any "magic" or hidden state that prevents external charging; once disconnected from the vehicle's electrical system, it behaves exactly like an isolated electrochemical cell waiting for a voltage differential.

From an engineering perspective, this process relies on fundamental principles of voltage and current flow rather than any proprietary car-specific logic. A standard lead-acid automotive battery sits at approximately 12 volts when fully charged. When you connect a running donor vehicle to the dead one via jumper cables, you are creating a parallel circuit. The alternator in the donor car is actively generating electricity (typically 13.5V to 14.5V under load), while the dead battery in your trunk sits at roughly 10 volts or less.

Because current always flows from higher potential to lower potential, electrons will naturally migrate from the donor vehicle's battery/alternator system into the depleted battery of your Miata. This flow continues until the voltage potentials equalize, effectively pushing ions back into the lead plates and restoring chemical energy. There is no need for the car to be running during a traditional jump-start scenario where you are trying to crank an engine; however, having the donor vehicle's engine running ensures the alternator is active and capable of delivering the amps needed to recharge the dead battery efficiently.

### Connection Order and Polarity Safety

The primary technical constraint in this operation is strict adherence to polarity. Connecting the red clamp (positive) to the positive terminal and the black clamp (negative) to the negative terminal is non-negotiable. Reversing these connections creates a short circuit across the donor vehicle's electrical system, which can instantly blow fuses, damage alternators, or in worst-case scenarios, cause sparks capable of igniting hydrogen gas emitted by any battery, regardless of whether it is dead or not.

When performing an external charge, the sequence of connection matters significantly for safety and component longevity. You must follow the standard industry protocol:
1.  Connect the red clamp to the positive (+) terminal of the donor vehicle.
2.  Connect the red clamp to the positive (+) terminal of the dead battery.
3.  Connect the black clamp to the negative (-) terminal of the donor vehicle.
4.  Connect the black clamp to an unpainted metal surface on the chassis of the dead car (a ground point). If you are charging a removed battery sitting on the ground, simply connect the negative clamp to the negative terminal of the dead battery if there are no other grounded metal parts nearby, though connecting to a known good ground strap is often preferred to avoid sparking near battery acid.

### The Role of the Alternator vs. Direct Battery-to-Battery

A common misconception is that you can charge a car battery by simply hooking it up to another dead battery without an engine running. While technically possible if one battery has residual charge, this method relies on the voltage differential between two static sources. If both batteries are fully discharged, no current will flow because there is no potential difference to drive the electrons.

Using a donor vehicle with its engine running utilizes the alternator, which acts as a regulated power supply. The alternator maintains a higher voltage (around 14V) regardless of the load. This ensures that even if your dead Miata battery only has 9 volts remaining, the system will actively push current into it. The charging rate is limited by the internal resistance of the dead battery and the maximum output amperage of the donor alternator. You might see a lower charge current compared to using a dedicated smart charger, but for a quick top-up to get you home or back in the trunk, it is highly effective.

### Practical Considerations for Removed Batteries

Since your specific scenario involves physically moving the battery out of the trunk, you are eliminating the physical obstruction that prevented jumper cable access. This changes the topology slightly: instead of bridging two vehicles while they are parked next to each other, you are now treating the dead battery as a standalone component being charged in parallel with the donor system.

Be aware that lead-acid batteries emit hydrogen gas during both discharge and charge cycles. Charging a removed battery increases this risk if done in an enclosed space. Ensure adequate ventilation. Furthermore, once the voltage of the two systems equalizes, the current draw will drop significantly. If you disconnect the cables too early while the donor alternator is still spinning at high RPMs, or if the dead battery has recovered enough voltage to nearly match the donor, the system stabilizes quickly.

There are no special electronic locks in a 1991 Miata that prevent this. The car's ECU will see no power once the battery is disconnected, effectively turning the vehicle into a mechanical sculpture until reconnected. If you plan to drive the Miata after this process, allow the alternator to run the engine for at least 30 minutes after reaching your destination to ensure the battery has had time to replenish its state of charge.
